planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this old Dutch heirloom, derived from wild Crocus flavus of the Balkans, is among the most vigorous and long-lived large-flowered crocus for naturalizing in lawns.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and about 3-4 inches apart in fall, in well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade; this 17th-century heirloom selection produces large, unmarked, rich buttercup-yellow goblets with glossy petals ahead of most other large crocus. It is exceptionally vigorous and long-lived, naturalizing readily in turf, gravel gardens, and under deciduous shrubs where it can be left undisturbed to multiply into broad drifts over years. The narrow grass-like leaves carry a faint silvery midstripe and should be left to yellow and wither naturally before mowing over naturalized plantings. Its tough constitution and reliable multiplication make it one of the best choices for a low-maintenance, long-term spring bulb display.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this Turkish species multiplies quickly into dense clusters and is among the very first crocus to open in late winter.

directions: Set corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, planting in fall for bloom in late winter to earliest spring. Native to the dry hillsides around Ankara, Turkey, each corm produces multiple small, deep golden-orange flowers held close together in a tight cluster, giving rise to the cultivar name. It multiplies rapidly by offsets to form dense, cheerful colonies in rock gardens, gravel beds, and the front of borders, often flowering while snow still patches the ground. Allow foliage to die back naturally before any mowing if naturalized in short turf.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun; flowers rise from bare ground within weeks of planting, ahead of the foliage.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun; native to olive groves and rocky ground near the coast of the southern Peloponnese, Greece, it sends up slender, long-tubed, softly scented lavender flowers with a paler throat directly from bare soil in October, well ahead of the narrow foliage that follows. It is one of the more tender fall crocus species and appreciates a hot, dry summer baking, making it a good choice for a raised bed, gravel garden, or bulb frame in regions with wet summers. Established colonies increase steadily by offsets and self-seeding where drainage is sharp.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; despite the common name it is native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia, not Scotland, and naturalizes well in short turf.

directions: Set corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in well-drained soil in full sun, planting in fall for bloom in late winter to early spring. Flowers open white to pale lilac-blue with a bright yellow throat, and the outer petals are often feathered or flushed with purple-bronze on the reverse, giving rise to the alternate name silvery crocus. Despite its common name, it is native not to Scotland but to a broad range from Italy and the Balkans through Turkey and the Caucasus. It naturalizes readily in lawns and rock gardens, multiplying by offsets, and its early, weather-tolerant blooms make it a dependable source of nectar for the season's first foraging bees.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; like other tommasinianus selections it naturalizes and self-seeds freely in lawns.

directions: Plant corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Barr's Purple is a richly colored selection of the woodland crocus, opening larger, deeper reddish-purple goblets than the species with a silvery-lilac reverse, on stems that appear among the earliest crocus of late winter. Like other Crocus tommasinianus cultivars it is more squirrel- and rodent-resistant than Dutch hybrid crocus, and it self-seeds and multiplies rapidly to form sizable colonies in lawns, under deciduous trees, and along woodland edges. Allow foliage to yellow completely before mowing over naturalized plantings.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in late summer in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; flowers emerge directly from bare soil in autumn before the leaves appear.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in late summer in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; native to Turkey, the Caucasus, and Iran, it sends up pale lilac-pink, long-tubed flowers with darker veining and a yellow throat directly from bare ground in October, well before the strap-like foliage follows. Unlike the closely related but toxic Colchicum, it is a true crocus with just three stamens and slender leaves, and is a genuine saffron relative safe to grow among edible plantings. It appreciates a dry summer rest and is well suited to naturalizing in short turf, gravel gardens, or beneath deciduous trees, multiplying readily into large autumn-flowering colonies.

common_name: Rose Surprise Lily (Electric Blue Spider Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; naked flower stalks rise in late summer before the foliage, which follows in fall and persists through winter.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; among the most cold-hardy Lycoris species, it produces umbels of fragrant, soft pink trumpet flowers unexpectedly tipped in an unusual electric blue at the tepal edges, opening on bare stalks in late summer before any foliage is present. The strap-like leaves emerge in fall, overwinter as a low rosette, and die back by early summer, so it pairs well with later-emerging perennials or groundcovers that can mask the disappearing foliage. Once established, clumps are best left undisturbed for several years, as flowering improves with congestion, and the bulbs multiply gradually into showy autumn colonies.

common_name: Chinese Golden Surprise Lily (Golden Hurricane Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; flowers appear on bare stalks in late summer, well before the strap-like winter foliage emerges.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; native to moist wooded slopes of central China and South Korea, it is one of the hardiest Lycoris and produces striking golden-yellow to orange-yellow spidery flowers with strongly recurved, wavy-edged tepals on bare stalks in late summer. The strap-like leaves follow after bloom, persist through winter, and die back by early summer, leaving the ground bare through the dormant season. It combines beautifully with red-flowered Lycoris radiata for a two-tone display in the fall garden, and established clumps should be left undisturbed for the best flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; this is one of the more cold-hardy Lycoris species and one of the tallest, with flower stalks nearing 3 feet.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; native to central China, this vigorous species is among the tallest and most cold-hardy in the genus, sending up bare, leafless stalks nearly 3 feet tall in late summer topped with large, trumpet-shaped flowers that typically open white with a soft pink flush, though wild populations range from white through yellow to pink. The strap-like foliage follows the flowers, persisting through winter before dying back in late spring ahead of a dry summer dormancy. Its height and vigor make it a strong architectural presence at the back of a border, and undisturbed clumps increase steadily over the years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; newly planted bulbs commonly skip a bloom cycle and may take one to two years to flower after transplanting.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light woodland shade; native to Japan, Korea, and China, it produces clusters of soft red-orange to apricot, spidery flowers on bare foot-tall stalks that seem to appear overnight in mid- to late summer, ahead of most other Lycoris species. Short, lily-like leaves emerge afterward and persist into early summer before going dormant. Newly planted bulbs commonly take one to two years to settle in and flower, so patience is needed, and established clumps should then be left undisturbed to build into a reliable summer display. It prefers slightly more shade and moisture than red spider lily, making it well suited to a woodland garden edge.
